newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany decides to slaughter British, Swiss cattle.
newsitem.headline: Germany decides to slaughter British, Swiss cattle.

text.p: German officials on Wednesday ordered the immediate slaughter of 5,200 British and Swiss cattle to calm public fears that a fresh case of mad cow disease could be the first involving an animal born in Germany.
The officials from the federal government and Germany's 16 regional states also ordered the 14,000 offspring of British and Swiss cattle in Germany to be placed under observation.

The new case of bongiform spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease set alarm bells ringing after the agriculture ministry said on Tuesday the calf, which died in December, had been born in Germany to a British mother.
The country's previous four BSE cases all involved animals from Britain.
But the officials, summoned to an emergency meeting in Bonn, said doubts had arisen about the origin of the Galloway cow in question.
"The circumstances in this case are not clear," said Franz-Josef Feiter, the state secretary in the argiculture ministry told a news conference after the meeting.
He said the ear-tag on the animal, which came from a farm near the western town of Hoexter, may have been changed at some point, making it difficult to ascertain its origin.
Officials will now carry out tests to try to determine the animal's origin.

The case was particularly baffling, Feiter said, as the cow's presumed mother had since given birth to another calf which appeared perfectly healthy. The mother, who was slaughtered last year, had also shown no signs of BSE.
"This would be the such first case of possible infection from mother to calf," Feiter said. "Such a case has not even come to light in Britain."
He said the culling of 2,600 cattle from Britain and around the same number from Switzerland would be rushed through under special legislation and would begin as soon as possible.
The animals' offspring -- 12,000 from British stock and 2,000 of Swiss origin -- would not be allowed to be sold or slaughtered while invesitigations continue, he said.

Britain and Switzerland are the two countries with the largest number of BSE cases. Britain alone has recorded around 165,000 in the last 10 years and slaughtered around one million animals in response to the problem.
Germany, where consumers are particularly sensitive to public health issues, has been at the forefront of countries wanting tough action over BSE.
Bonn took a tough stance last year after Britain admitted a likely link between BSE and its human equivalent, the deadly brain-wasting Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).
Germany was in the vanguard of countries that demanded -- and got -- a worldwide ban on British beef and its by-products.
It has refused to agree to any easing of the export ban, even passing its own legislation to block an EU decision allowing Britain to resume exports of bull semen.
